If you only remember one thing today: A I became a campaign issue, and the industry's big political spending got mixed results at the ballot box.

Number one. The midterms and A I money.

Tuesday's midterm elections are in, and A I was a real theme. Several A I industry and A I safety political groups spent millions. The results were mixed. Two industry-aligned groups, American Mission and Building the Future, put about four point eight million dollars behind a South Carolina Senate candidate, Darlene Graham. She lost. American Mission also spent over half a million each on Republicans in Montana and North Carolina, and both lost. On the other side, a group called Guardrails Alliance helped defeat Representative Jimmy Gomez in California. And Public First, which is backed by Anthropic, put three million dollars behind state senator Scott Wiener, who was leading at last report. The big industry group Leading the Future spent more than twenty seven million dollars in primaries, and says it will keep spending through twenty twenty eight. From your Reads, Tech Policy Press is hosting a live podcast today at two P M Eastern on what the midterms mean for U S tech policy.

Why it matters: voters, not just lobbyists, are now shaping A I policy, and big spending is no guarantee of influence.

Number two. The frontier model race.

Google released Gemini four Carbon this week. Independent benchmarker Artificial Analysis ranks it first, at fifty nine on its index. Claude Opus five point five is right behind at fifty eight, and OpenAI's G P T six Astra at fifty seven. It also scored best on hallucination tests, though even the best score is only fifty four on a scale to one hundred, so reliability is still limited. Google is giving access first to cyber defenders. Meanwhile, OpenAI launched G P T six point one Terra, which can see a screen and act across apps, at half the price of its predecessor. And on October twenty sixth, Anthropic filed with the S E C to go public on Nasdaq under the ticker A N T, reporting about sixteen billion dollars in first half revenue. No shares can be sold until the filing takes effect.

Why it matters: the top three labs are separated by a point or two, so price, speed, and trust are now the real competition.

Number three. Nvidia and China.

Reports say Nvidia is telling its data center partners to cap Chinese customers at forty nine percent of their business, so at least fifty one percent is non-Chinese. It's a way to limit China's access to A I computing through overseas data centers.

Why it matters: the chip fight is moving from borders to the cloud, where it's harder to police.

Number four. Kids, chatbots, and new rules.

New York Governor Kathy Hochul signed a law on October twenty eighth restricting A I chatbots for anyone under eighteen. It bans bots posing as human, encouraging self harm, or having sexual conversations. Companies must verify age with more than one method, and the attorney general can seek up to twenty five thousand dollars per violation.

Why it matters: states are writing the rules for A I and kids while Washington debates.

Number five. Also in your Reads.

From The Comms Stack: fluency is camouflage. A I writes smoothly, so wrong facts slip through. The tip: ask the A I to list every factual claim in a draft, then check those separately. Deloitte's refund to the Australian government over fake citations is the cautionary tale. And The New Yorker's newsletter today looks at the midterm results, under the headline, America's Revenge.

Good news close. In open source, Mistral released the full weights of its one trillion parameter Large four model, so organizations can run it on their own hardware.

The thread today: A I is moving from the lab into elections, rulebooks, and supply chains. That's your briefing. Have a good day, Sin.
